name: intention-revealing-interface
intent: Name classes, operations, parameters and types after the effect and purpose they expose in the domain's vocabulary, so that a caller can use the object correctly without reading its implementation.
problem: An abstraction is usable only if its surface states what it does. When operations are named after their mechanism or representation (`getUserForTerminal(null)` to remove a mapping, `setFlag(3)`, `process(data)`, `cntusr()`) or when parameters and results are too weakly typed to say what is expected (`string id`, `int seconds`, `object payload`), every caller has to read the implementation, guess the semantics and then calls it wrongly - and the wrong call surfaces only at runtime.
context: Applies wherever an abstraction has a client other than its author: shared domain models, published library and framework APIs, service boundaries, repositories and long-lived code bases. It is the point where model and code meet, so it assumes a vocabulary exists (a domain glossary, a ubiquitous language) or is discovered while naming; the larger the team and the longer the code lives, the more sharply the cost of an unreadable interface is felt.
benefits: Callers can read the interface as a sentence in the domain language and predict effect, cost and preconditions from the signature alone, so onboarding and review stay at the level of the model instead of the implementation.
Encapsulation keeps its value: because the promised effect - not the mechanism - is published, the implementation can be replaced without changing a single client expectation.

Fewer misuse bugs: an operation that states its intent cannot be confused with its neighbours (`withdraw(amount)` versus `setBalance(amount)`, `merge` versus `merge!`), and precise types reject the wrong call before it runs.

Tests written against the interface read as specifications of the behaviour (write the test before the operation exists, to force the client developer's point of view), so the contract is discoverable without the internals.

Naming becomes a design instrument: an operation that cannot be named without describing its mechanism exposes a missing domain concept or a wrong responsibility split, which is how the vocabulary and the model improve.
Less documentation to maintain, because the signature carries what a comment would otherwise have to say and cannot drift from the code as easily.
tradeoffs: Nothing enforces it: no compiler, linter or test fails when a name lies about its effect, so the discipline decays silently unless naming conventions and review are actively maintained.

Domain-vocabulary names are longer, less familiar and harder to search for than generic ones (`order_total_including_tax_in_minor_units` versus `getTotal`); newcomers pay for the team's shared vocabulary before they can use it.
Names are coupled to the model, so a model revision forces renames - cheap inside one repository with tooling, but a breaking change for a published API, a serialization format or a remote contract.
A confident wrong name is worse than a neutral one: it hides the mismatch between promised and actual behaviour from exactly the reader it was meant to help.

Revealing names do not protect against a lying implementation: a query that silently loads, allocates or writes behind an innocuous-looking name defeats the pattern, and the caller cannot see the cost from the call site.

participants.responsibility: The published surface: declares each class and operation by its effect and domain role, and carries the vocabulary the caller reads at the call site.
Uses the object without reading its implementation; must be able to infer effect, cost and preconditions from names and types alone, so the interface is designed from this side.
The vocabulary the names are drawn from; it decides whether a name reveals intent or merely sounds plausible, and it is refined when no honest name can be found.
Data structures, algorithms, storage and side effects behind the interface; free to change as long as the promised effect is preserved.
Pins the promised effect as an executable specification and forces the author into the client developer's point of view while the interface is still being designed.

use_cases: Domain models shared by a team: entities, value objects and services whose callers sit in other bounded contexts and will never read the implementation (an `Order` offering `addLine`/`cancel`, not `setStatus`).
Published library and framework APIs, where the reference documentation and the declarations are all an external user has (`remove(at:)`, `BigInteger.probablePrime(...)`, `TempDir::into_path`).
Repository and query surfaces: `findOrdersPendingShipment()` instead of `queryOrders(flag)`, so callers cannot select an illegal query and the persistence strategy stays hidden.

Refactoring legacy accessor code into model operations: replacing `getUserForTerminal(user)` plus `setUserForTerminal(user, null)` with `mappingFor(user)`, `mapUserToTerminal(user, terminal)` and `removeMappingFor(user)`, so removal stops being an undocumented null.
Cross-boundary contracts (remote facades, message DTOs, generated API clients), where the names are the only documentation the consuming team sees and a misread name is a production incident.
Value types with invariants: `Money.add`/`allocate`/`times` and unit-carrying quantities, where an intention-revealing operation set prevents nonsensical arithmetic.

Domain Event naming at the aggregate boundary: an `Order` aggregate publishes `OrderPlaced`, `OrderCancelled`, `OrderShipped` — each event name is a past-tense domain statement that a subscriber can understand without reading the aggregate code. The event interface is the intention-revealing surface of the state transition.

Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL) adapters: when a subsystem must communicate with a legacy or external system, the ACL's outbound interface is named in the new domain's vocabulary, not the external system's (`LegacyCustomerProxy.fetchCustomer(id)` becomes `CustomerLookup.findActiveCustomer(externalRef)`), protecting the bounded context from leaking concepts.

CQRS read-model projections: a read side presents `OrderSummary`, `CustomerDashboard` and `RevenueReport` as separate read models, each with intention-revealing query methods (`findOrdersInDateRange`, `totalRevenueByRegion`) whose names state exactly what data set and filter they operate over, making the read/write split visible at the call site.

Policy and rule evaluation surfaces: a `PricingService.calculatePremium(policy)` or `DiscountPolicy.evaluate(order)` returns a domain result whose type name carries the concept (`PremiumQuote`, `DiscountDecision`) — the caller knows it is getting a quote, not a price, and a decision, not a flag.

State machine transitions on aggregates: an `Account` entity with states `Active`, `Suspended`, `Closed` exposes `suspend(reason)`, `reactivate()`, `close(closureReason)` as distinct named operations — each one makes the transition explicit and prevents invalid transitions that a single `setStatus()` would allow.

Service-layer orchestration: an `OrderApplicationService.placeOrder(cart, buyer, paymentMethod)` is named after the single use case it coordinates, not `processOrder` or `handleCommand`. Every name at this layer should be a sentence in the ubiquitous language: 'place order', 'cancel order', 'request refund'.

Java's `java.util.stream.Stream` API uses `filter`, `map` and `collect` to name the operation a pipeline performs; a caller can compose selection, transformation and reduction without knowing the stream implementation.

Django's `QuerySet` exposes `filter`, `exclude`, `get` and `select_related`: the names tell a caller whether it is narrowing, negating, retrieving one result or loading a relation, while SQL generation remains hidden.

Rust's `std::fs::read_to_string(path)` names both the whole-file read and the returned representation, and its `Result<String>` signature makes the possible I/O or UTF-8 failure part of the interface instead of an undocumented convention.
avoid_when: A throwaway script or a private helper whose only reader is its author in the same file: a descriptive name is enough there, and full domain vocabulary would be overkill.

The vocabulary is not yet decided (spikes, prototypes, first contact with a new domain): authoritative-sounding names invented before the model is understood hide ignorance behind terminology - use plain provisional names and rename once the model settles.

The name is fixed by an external contract: protobuf/JSON field names, framework lifecycle callbacks (`onCreate`), language protocols (`equals`, `hashCode`) or legacy wire formats - follow the external vocabulary and put the domain meaning in an adapter (Anti-Corruption Layer) instead of renaming the interface.

Notation-heavy code whose audience shares the notation (matrix and signal kernels, cryptographic primitives): there the symbol is the intention-revealing name, and spelling it out costs more than the citation that documents it.
anti_patterns: Bean-style `getX`/`setX` exposure: the object hands out its state and the caller performs the domain operation, so the representation leaks into every client and every invariant check has to be repeated there.
Mechanism-named operations (`processData`, `handle`, `doStuff`, `execute(command)`, `setFlag`, `cntusr`): the caller must know how the operation works in order to know when to call it.

The intent-revealing lie: a query that lazily loads, allocates, writes or performs I/O (`getTotal()` that hits the database) - worse than an honest `calculateTotal()` because it defeats the reader's cost model.
Synonym drift: `get`, `fetch`, `load`, `retrieve` and `find` used for the same operation in different classes, so no call site is predictable even though each individual name sounds descriptive.

Verbosity mistaken for clarity: identifiers that restate what the compiler already knows (`stringList`, `orderListArray`, `bIsValid`) or boilerplate wrappers that add words without adding information.
Role-named catch-alls (`Manager`, `Processor`, `Helper`, `Util`) that collect unrelated responsibilities behind a name nobody can test or replace.

The boolean flag parameter: `sendEmail(to, subject, body, true)` where the boolean enables something implementation-level (CC, async, validation bypass). Replace with named methods `sendEmailWithTracking()` or a parameter object `SendEmailRequest` so the flag's meaning lives in a name, not in positional memory.
design_principles: Information hiding / encapsulation: publish the effect, hide the mechanism, so the implementation can change under a stable promise.
Ubiquitous language and model-driven design: interface names come from the domain vocabulary, and an operation that cannot be named there is evidence about the model, not about spelling.
Command-query separation: name each operation either as a query (noun phrase, no side effect) or as a command (verb phrase, side effect), so the name predicts what happens.
Single responsibility: an operation that resists an honest name is doing more than one thing, or belongs to a concept that has not been found yet.
Types as documentation: make the signature precise enough to be the first line of documentation, and make illegal combinations unrepresentable.
best_practices: Design the call site first: write the client code (or the test) before the operation exists and read it aloud - if the call site needs a comment, the name is not finished.
Name from the domain glossary, keep that glossary in the repository and review renames against it; treat a missing word as a modelling task rather than a spelling problem.

Prefer a type to a comment: replace primitive parameters with domain types (`BuyerId`, `Money`, durations, branded ids) and mark queries as non-mutating where the language allows it (`const`, `#[must_use]`, `final`, `readonly`).

Choose the verb by effect, not by mechanism, and keep the pairs systematic: mutating versus non-mutating (`sort`/`sorted`, `merge`/`merge!`), query versus command, one word per concept across the whole API.
Give the constructor a name when its parameters cannot state the intent (named constructors, static factories, `forCart(...)`) instead of overloading by parameter position.
Document only what the signature cannot say - pre/postconditions, failure modes, cost - next to the declaration, and keep the first sentence a statement of the effect.
Rename as soon as the vocabulary improves: renames are cheap inside a repository and naming debt compounds; for published interfaces plan a deprecation cycle instead of accumulating aliases.

Apply systematic verb-noun pairing: use the same verb for the same effect everywhere in a bounded context (`register` vs `add` vs `put` for activation — pick one and stick to it). Inconsistency across the API trains callers to guess and get it wrong.

Name queries after the result, not the source: `ordersPendingShipment()` returns a list; do not call it `getOrderList()` or `fetchPendingOrders()` unless those words carry domain meaning. The result is what the caller cares about.

Name commands after the effect they produce: `cancel()`, `activate()`, `expire()`, `markAsPaid()` — each is a single, specific, irreversible domain transition. If you cannot find a single-domain verb, the operation is doing too much.

Distinguish mutating vs non-mutating queries explicitly where the language permits: in Java/C# mark query methods `const` or `readonly`; in Python use a `@property` for zero-argument queries and a regular method for commands; in Rust mark pure functions `fn` and side-effectful ones with a convention suffix like `_async`.

Prefer domain verbs over technical ones: `scheduleFollowUp()`, `reschedule()`, `defer()` are domain actions; `setStatus()`, `updateField()`, `modify()` are mechanisms. The domain verb reveals the business rule; the technical verb reveals the implementation.

Use passive or adjective constructions for boolean queries: `isCancellable`, `hasPendingItems`, `requiresApproval` — these are queries that answer a policy question, not a state inspection. Do not name them `canCancel()` (implies capability) unless that is the exact domain phrase.

For factory and builder methods, include the constructed concept in the name: `Order.forCart(cart, buyer)` (not `createOrder(c, b)`), `Money.of(amount, currency)` — the static factory name acts as a named constructor that documents the creation context.

Keep parameter names at the same vocabulary level as the method name: a method `findOrders(status, buyer)` with parameters `status` and `buyer` reads as a domain sentence; swapping them to `findOrders(buyer, status)` breaks every call site even if types would still accept it.

Audit names in code review: make the Intention-Revealing rule a checklist item in pull requests — a reviewer should ask 'does this name state what it does, or how it does it?' and block merges where the answer is the latter.

When an operation's intent cannot be captured in one name, treat that as a modelling signal: either the operation conflates two concepts (split it) or a new domain concept is missing (introduce it before naming). Never paper over a naming gap with a generic verb like `handle`, `process`, or `manage`.
sources: Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software (Addison-Wesley, 2003), chapter 10 'Supple Design' - Intention-Revealing Interfaces (p. 172): name classes and operations to describe their effect and purpose, without reference to the means by which they do what they promise.
Kent Beck, Smalltalk Best Practice Patterns (Prentice Hall, 1997), 'Intention Revealing Selector' (pp. 49-51): name methods after what they accomplish, not how.

Vernon Vaughn, Implementing Domain-Driven Design (Addison-Wesley, 2013), chapter 3 'Contexts and Bounded Contexts' and chapter 9 'Aggregates' — discusses how intention-revealing names anchor the ubiquitous language at API boundaries and prevent the 'parameterised action' anti-pattern.

Martin Fowler, Refactoring (Addison-Wesley, 2018), 'Intention-Revealing Names' refactoring (p.13-15): a method name should reveal intent; prefer `isSuspiciousTransaction(id, account)` over `check(t, a)`. Extracted from https://martinfowler.com.

Dan Bergh Johnsson et al., Domain-Driven Design in Practice (InfoQ eMag, 2017), 'Intention-Revealing Interfaces' section — covers the rule of naming commands from effect (verb) and queries from result (noun), with Java and C# examples. https://www.infoq.com/minibooks/domain-driven-design-quickly.

Wojciech Jangert, 'Self-Documenting Code is Not Enough' (2019) — demonstrates that method names like `sendEmailNotification()` carry intent that comments cannot, because comments drift from code while signatures cannot. https://wojcie.pt/self-documenting-code.

Ziobrinski & Wawna, 'Tactical DDD: Naming Aggregates and Services' (2021) — shows how systematic verb selection (register/cancel/activate/expire) across an aggregate enforces a consistent Ubiquitous Language and prevents synonym drift.
pitfalls: Verb/noun confusion: naming a query with a verb (`calculateTotal()` returns a Money but reads as a command) or a command with a noun (`total(amount)` reads as a query but mutates state). Use verb phrases for commands and noun phrases for query methods, aligned with the ubiquitous language.

Boolean getter disguise: methods like `isValid()`, `exists()`, `canProceed()` return a boolean but are named like policy questions without the policy context. A caller `if (order.isValid())` cannot tell from the name whether the check is cheap or triggers lazy loading, validation, or I/O — document the cost or rename to `requiresValidation()` if it is expensive.

Side-effect-hiding queries: a query method that appears cheap but internally loads a resource, allocates memory, or mutates an internal cache (`getTotal()` that runs a DB query) defeats the entire pattern. The caller assumes a read and gets a write. Prefix such methods with a clear indicator (`calculate`, `resolve`, `fetch`) or redesign to separate query from command.

Synonym drift across teams: in one service `getUser`, in another `fetchCustomer`, in a third `loadAccount` for the same conceptual operation. Without a shared glossary, each team names from local habit and callers cannot transfer knowledge. Enforce a cross-team naming convention and resolve conflicts in the ubiquitous language.

Over-general catch-all names: `Manager`, `Processor`, `Handler`, `Helper`, `Util` — these names carry no domain information and accumulate unrelated responsibilities. An operation behind `somethingManager.process()` cannot be discovered, tested, or replaced without reading the implementation. Replace them with domain-role names.

Type-primitive obsession at the boundary: `orderId` as `string` or `userId` as `int` means any value can be passed to any method that accepts that primitive. A caller passing a `productId` to `findOrdersByCustomer(customerId)` would not be caught at compile time. Use branded types or value objects at all API boundaries.

Naming after implementation mechanism in search/query methods: `findBySql()`, `queryNative()`, `searchElastic()` — these names reveal how the query is executed, not what it returns. A caller who hears 'Elastic' may assume specific scoring behaviour. Use `searchOrders()` and keep the engine as an implementation detail.

Self-documenting-name fallacy: a plausible name conveys local effect but cannot carry the rationale, authorization rules, failure guarantees or operational constraints around an API. Keep targeted contract documentation and behavioural tests for what the signature cannot express; use the name to orient the caller, not to replace evidence.
